- **Static sag: 35 mm (1.38 in)** — bike upright under its own weight, no rider.
- **Rider sag: 105 mm (4.13 in)** — you seated in full riding gear, feet on the pegs.

Measure both as the drop from the rear suspension fully extended, using the rear axle and the same rear-fender SAG mark each time. Set rider sag first, then check static sag: too little static sag with correct rider sag points to a shock spring that’s too soft; too much points to one that’s too stiff.

That combination often means the fork is **riding too deep in its stroke**, where it feels harsh on chop but has little travel left for landings. Simply softening compression can make both worse.

1. **Fork air:** check it cold with the front wheel off the ground; GasGas’s stock reference is **10.4 bar (151 psi)**. Record the existing pressure before correcting it. Bleed the outer chambers through their bleeder screws—not the main air-spring valve.
2. **Fork compression:** if it dives and uses lots of travel even on ordinary hits, go **2 clicks in from your current position** for more hold-up. GasGas’s standard reference is **12 clicks out**; if you’re there now, test **10 out**. Leave rebound unchanged.

Does it ride high and deflect on the small chop, or dive and stay deep?

Test the pressure correction first, then the compression change separately over the same section. Keep the firmer compression only if chop comfort and landing support both improve; otherwise return to your recorded setting. If it stays high over chop yet still bottoms, check fork alignment and service condition before chasing more damping.

**Changes to try, one at a time:**
- **Fork air pressure:** Check cold with the front wheel off the ground; use 10.4 bar (151 psi) as the stock reference, recording the existing pressure first.
Harshness plus bottoming can mean the fork is too soft and riding deep—not too stiff. Check cold air pressure before opening the compression clicker.

Your fork needs more braking support—**check its air spring before adding compression damping**.

1. **Fork air:** with the fork cold and front wheel off the ground, check against GasGas’s stock reference of **10.4 bar (151 psi)**. If it’s below that, restore it and retest before changing clickers. Release trapped outer-chamber air through the bleeder screws—not the main air valve.
2. **Fork compression:** if pressure is correct, turn compression **2 clicks inward from your current position**. If you’re at the stock 12 clicks out, try **10 out**. Leave rebound unchanged; its stock reference is 12 out.

Repeat the same braking zone for a few laps. You want less dive without the front becoming harsh or pushing wide; undo the compression change if either happens. Also verify **105 mm riding sag and 35 mm static sag**, because a rear riding too high loads the fork.

For technique, set your standing position before braking: hips back over the pegs, knees gripping, then squeeze rather than grab the front brake. Practice five controlled straight-line stops at an easy pace.

**One click at a time** is the best testing step on your 2022 CRF250R—testers consistently find this generation sensitive to small adjustments. Two clicks can help make the difference obvious, but use one click to fine-tune.

Write down your starting position, change only one adjuster, then ride the same section for a few laps at a similar pace. If it gets worse, return to your starting setting before trying something else.

Clicks are counted out from lightly seated: **in adds damping; out reduces damping**. Compression controls resistance to compressing; rebound controls return speed. A shock high-speed compression adjuster that turns rather than clicks needs to be tracked in fractions of a turn.
Change one click at a time on your CRF250R, testing one adjuster at a time.

**Fine cold, then soft and bouncy after 20 minutes points to shock damping fading as it heats up.** A little change with temperature is expected; losing control of the rear is not.

Most likely, in order:
- **Oil degradation or aeration:** hot oil provides less damping, and foaming makes rebound control inconsistent.
- **Low nitrogen pressure or a reservoir sealing fault:** allows aeration as the shock works. If the rear also sits lower after riding, Honda specifically calls for checking nitrogen loss.
- **Worn internal seals or piston band:** oil bypass increases as everything warms up.

First, with the bike cold and engine off, inspect the shock shaft, seal head and reservoir for oil wetness or damage. A dry shock can still have an internal fault. Don’t chase this with firmer clickers—it can hide the hot problem and make it harsh cold.

How many riding hours since the shock was last serviced? **If the rear is bouncing repeatedly or losing dependable control, stop riding until the shock is checked; nitrogen testing and charging need suspension-service equipment.**
That points to heat-related damping fade, not a spring or clicker problem. Inspect for leakage, then have the shock’s oil, nitrogen charge and internal sealing checked.

Yes—the tires absorb the first part of every bump, so pressure can make the suspension feel firmer or softer without touching a clicker.

- **Higher pressure:** firmer feel, more feedback and deflection over chop, but better rim protection on sharp hits.
- **Lower pressure:** more compliance and grip, but too low feels vague or squirmy and risks pinch flats and rim damage.

Honda’s baseline for your 2023 CRF450R is **100 kPa (15 psi) cold, front and rear**. Establish that before judging the suspension.

As general tuning practice, try about **1 psi at a time**: lower for smooth, slick ground or deep sand; higher for rocks, square edges and hard landings. Change one end at a time and ride the same section. Stop lowering pressure if you feel a rim strike or tire squirm. Pressure changes tire cushioning—not the fork or shock’s actual damping.

**Your shock spring is likely too soft for your weight.** With rider sag correct at **105 mm (4.13 in)**, GasGas calls for **35 mm (1.38 in) static sag**—your 20 mm is too little.

Assuming the measurements repeat and the linkage moves freely, you’ve needed too much spring preload to hold yourself up. When you get off, that preload pushes the rear almost fully extended.

The usual fix is a **stiffer shock spring**, then resetting rider sag to 105 mm and checking that static sag comes close to 35 mm. Backing off preload alone will increase static sag, but also leave too much rider sag; clickers won’t correct the spring mismatch.

Before buying a spring, repeat both measurements, settling the rear from above and below. A noticeably different result points to linkage or seal friction that needs checking first.
Your shock spring is likely too soft: it needs excessive preload to achieve 105 mm rider sag, leaving only 20 mm static sag.

With the **standard shock spring 56 N/mm**, too much preload means compressing its installed length below **222.9 mm (8.78 in)**—measure the spring itself, seat to seat, with the rear wheel off the ground.

Honda’s figures are:
- Standard installed length: **232.3 mm (9.15 in)**.
- Allowed installed length: **222.9–233 mm (8.78–9.20 in)**.
- One adjuster turn shortens the spring by **1.5 mm**, adding **84 N** of preload—not 1.5 mm of rider-sag change.

Aim for **105 mm rider sag**, measured seated in normal riding position with full gear. If you cannot reach that before the spring reaches minimum length, fit a stiffer spring rather than tightening farther; Honda’s optional stiff shock spring is **58 N/mm**.

Also check free sag with the rider off: very little free sag at correct rider sag indicates a spring that’s too soft. Honda publishes no free-sag target for this bike; **30–40 mm is general tuning guidance**, not Honda’s specification. Preload raises ride height; it does not increase the spring’s rate.
On your 2023 CRF450R’s standard shock spring, preload is excessive if the installed spring length is shorter than 222.9 mm. Sag can show that you need a stiffer spring before reaching that limit.

Most ride-to-ride sag changes come from **measurement differences, suspension friction, or preload collars moving**—not the spring suddenly getting softer.

On your 2022 CRF250R, Honda’s standard rider sag is **105 mm (4.1 in) with the standard shock spring 50 N/mm**.

Check these in order:
1. **Same measuring conditions:** same riding gear, fuel load, body position and helper; clean accumulated mud off first. Measure between the left rear-fender bolt center and chain-adjuster locknut center, comparing rear-wheel-off-ground with rider aboard.
2. **Check for friction:** with you aboard, have your helper settle the rear once from pushing down and once from lifting up. Different resting measurements point toward sticky linkage, swingarm bearings or shock seals. Don’t keep chasing that with preload.
3. **Mark the preload collars:** a witness mark shows whether they move between rides. Fresh suspension can also settle during break-in.

Honda does not publish a static-sag target for this bike; **30–40 mm is general guidance**, checked after rider sag is set. Hot damping oil changes how quickly the rear settles, not its final resting sag by itself.

How many millimeters is it changing? Start with the repeatability check before turning the collars.
Changing measurement conditions or suspension friction are more likely than the spring changing rate. Repeat the measurement consistently before adjusting preload again.

On your 2023 CRF450R, **bleed built-up fork air after practice and between motos**, with the **front wheel off the ground and forks fully extended**.

1. Shut the engine off and support the bike securely on a stand so the front wheel hangs free.
2. Wipe dirt away from the small air-release screw on top of each fork leg.
3. Slowly loosen each air-release screw until any trapped air stops hissing. Don’t loosen the large fork caps.
4. Gently retighten both screws—don’t crank them down.

These are coil-spring forks: you’re releasing unwanted pressure, not setting an air-spring pressure. Trapped pressure can make the fork feel firmer and harsher.

I can also walk you through **Release built-up air from the fork**; tap **“Working on the bike?”** above the message box. Have a stand and a screwdriver that fits the release screws ready.
Release built-up fork air after practice and between motos, with the front wheel off the ground and the forks fully extended.

**Internal air-side service means servicing the left air-spring cartridge—not just bleeding the fork.** Don’t pour the outer-leg oil quantity into the sealed air cartridge.

**Clickers adjust the damping you already have; a revalve changes how that damping builds through a hit.**

- **Clickers** usually adjust an oil bypass or valve preload. Their effects overlap: opening compression for comfort can also lose braking support or bottoming resistance.

The payoff is fixing conflicting demands: **more comfort over chop while keeping support under braking and on landings**, or faster recovery through repeated bumps without a springy kick after one big hit. It isn’t unlimited independent adjustment, but it gives the tuner much more control.

**The main difference is what holds the bike up: compressed air versus a steel coil spring.** Both still use oil to control how fast the fork moves.

- **Air fork:** A piston compresses trapped air as the fork goes down. The smaller that air space gets, the harder it pushes back, so resistance builds toward full travel. A negative-air chamber helps counter the initial force and lets the fork start moving more easily.
- **Coil-spring fork:** A steel spring compresses as the fork moves. A straight-rate spring adds roughly the same amount of force for each additional inch of travel. Trapped air above the oil still adds bottoming resistance near the end.
- **Damping in both:** Pistons force oil through passages and flexible shim stacks. Compression damping controls the inward stroke; rebound damping controls the return. Air pressure or spring rate is separate from those adjustments.

Your MC 250F’s **WP XACT AER uses the left leg for the air spring and the right for the damping cartridge**. GasGas’s stock air setting is **10.4 bar (151 psi), checked cold**. Air lets you change spring support with a pump; a coil fork needs a different spring to change its rate.
An air fork replaces the steel coil spring with a sealed air piston and chambers. Both designs still use oil damping to control compression and rebound.

**Compression tells you how much pressure the engine builds; leak-down helps tell you where it loses it.**

- **Compression test:** A gauge records pressure while you crank the engine. It’s a quick overall check, but cranking speed, valve timing and an automatic decompressor can affect the reading—not just worn rings or leaking valves.
- **Leak-down test:** With the piston held at top dead center on the compression stroke and both valves closed, a tester feeds regulated air into the cylinder and indicates leakage. Listening for escaping air helps locate the problem:
  - Intake: intake-valve leakage.
  - Exhaust: exhaust-valve leakage.
  - Crankcase breather: leakage past the rings; some is normal.
  - Bubbles in coolant: possible head-gasket leakage or a crack into the cooling system.

So a low compression reading alone doesn’t prove the top end is worn out. Leak-down helps separate valve sealing from ring/cylinder sealing, though it won’t identify every timing or oil-consumption problem.

**Squish is the gap between the piston crown and the outer band of the cylinder head when the piston reaches the top of its stroke.** On your YZ125, that band squeezes the fuel-air mixture inward toward the spark plug as the piston comes up.

|---|---|---|
